html:
From about 985 Norse settlers led by Erik the Red farmed the fjords of south west Greenland in two colonies, the Eastern and Western Settlements. At their height perhaps 2,000 to 3,000 people lived there.

They kept cattle, sheep and goats, built stone churches, and from 1126 had their own bishop at Gardar. Their main export was walrus ivory, sent to Norway and on to Europe. From Greenland they reached North America.

The Western Settlement was empty by about 1350 and the Eastern by the mid 1400s, after the last record from Hvalsey. Causes are debated: the cooling of the Little Ice Age, a fall in the ivory trade, isolation from Norway and contact with the Thule Inuit.
